$comment: The twenty-three must-never rules. Standard 25. Each rule's `title` is the source text VERBATIM — scripts/inventory.mjs holds the same strings and fails the build if one is reworded, so softening a prohibition here cannot pass review. Everything else in each entry is authored.
$exemptibility: Exactly four are nonExemptible: guaranteed-returns and the three fabrication rules. No project context makes those acceptable — inventing a price, a balance, or a tax rule corrupts the evidence every downstream conclusion rests on, and a guarantee claim asserts the absence of a risk the reader cannot check for. The other nineteen are materiality and context judgements a policy may legitimately scope. Making all twenty-three unwaivable was considered and rejected in Standard 25 R4: a stop signal that fires constantly is one people learn to route around.
$assurance: Three rules have lexical detectors and claim `partial`. Twenty are `manual-review` with `assurance: none` — including all three fabrication rules, because no scan establishes that a figure was NOT invented without already knowing the true value. That is uncomfortable and it is stated rather than softened: the most consequential prohibitions in this domain are the least checkable. `guaranteed-returns` joined them on measured evidence rather than on principle: candidate replay 01 established that no lexical scan can decide whether a guarantee claim's subject is an investment return. Its DISCOVERY half survives as `review.guarantee-language-present`, which surfaces the passages and adjudicates nothing.

rules.title: describe investment returns as guaranteed
rules.description: The analysis describes an investment return as guaranteed, assured, certain, risk-free, or promised.
rules.rationale: A guarantee claim is not an overstatement of degree. It asserts the absence of a risk that is present, and it is the one claim a reader cannot verify for themselves — which is why no context makes it acceptable.
rules.remediation: State the return as an assumption or a scenario, with its downside case. If an instrument genuinely carries a contractual guarantee, name the guarantor and the conditions, because the guarantee is only as good as they are.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Deciding this requires establishing that the guaranteed thing is an INVESTMENT RETURN, and candidate replay 01 measured that a lexical scan cannot: the framework's own clearest violation names no investment anywhere in the document, while a correct published comparison names twenty-one. Vocabulary is at best uncorrelated with the violation. So this reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person reads the passages and records the judgement with evidence. `review.guarantee-language-present` finds the passages and can never establish this rule — discovery is not adjudication, and a run that reported this as passing because a scan found nothing would be the framework committing the error it exists to catch.

rules.title: fabricate market data
rules.description: A price, index level, yield, return, or other market figure is stated without being drawn from a real source.
rules.rationale: Every conclusion downstream of a fabricated figure is computed from a number that describes nothing. The analysis is not merely wrong — it is unfalsifiable, because there is no source against which to check it.
rules.remediation: Cite the source and as-of date for every market figure, or mark it as an assumption rather than a fact. Where the figure is needed but unavailable, mark it [requires current external data] and state what the conclusion depends on.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED, and cannot be. Establishing that a figure was not invented requires the true value, which is what the document was supposed to supply. This reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person checks the sources and records the judgement. A run that reported it as passing because nothing was found would be this framework committing the error it exists to catch.

rules.title: fabricate account data
rules.description: A balance, holding, contribution, transaction, or other account figure is stated without being drawn from the actual account.
rules.rationale: An analysis of someone's finances built on invented balances is an analysis of a person who does not exist, presented to a person who does.
rules.remediation: Take account figures from statements, and state the as-of date. Where a figure is unknown, mark it [requires personal financial context] and treat the analysis as conditional on it rather than filling it in.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED, and cannot be. No check available here can distinguish a real balance from a plausible one. Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person confirms the figures against the source records.

rules.title: fabricate tax rules
rules.description: A rate, threshold, allowance, relief, or rule of tax law is stated without being drawn from the actual law of the relevant jurisdiction.
rules.rationale: Tax rules are jurisdiction-specific, change annually, and are exactly the kind of detail a reader will not independently check. An invented one produces a number that is wrong in a way that only shows up when it is acted on.
rules.remediation: Cite the jurisdiction, the tax year, and the source for every rate or threshold. Where the applicable rules are unknown, mark it [requires personal financial context] — jurisdiction and circumstances determine which rules apply at all.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED, and cannot be. Verifying a tax rule requires the law, which this repository does not carry and which changes without notice. Reports NOT_EVALUATED until a person confirms it against the source.

rules.title: hide assumptions
rules.description: A figure the conclusion depends on is embedded in the analysis without being stated as an assumption a reader can see and disagree with.
rules.rationale: An assumption the reader cannot see is one they cannot challenge. Hidden assumptions are how a projection acquires the authority of a calculation while resting on a guess.
rules.remediation: List every input the conclusion is sensitive to in an assumptions section, with its value and its basis.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated but not established by disclosure.assumptions-section, which detects whether such a section EXISTS. Whether it lists every load-bearing assumption is a judgement about what the analysis actually depends on, and no checker makes it.

rules.title: ignore fees when material
rules.description: Returns or projected values are presented without accounting for fees, where the fees would materially change the conclusion.
rules.rationale: Fee drag is small per period, always in one direction, and compounds — the shape of error that is easiest to dismiss and most expensive to carry.
rules.remediation: State the fees and present figures net of them. Where fees are genuinely immaterial or absent, say so rather than omitting the subject.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by disclosure.fees-accounted, which detects whether fees are mentioned at all. Materiality is a judgement: whether the omitted fees WOULD have changed the conclusion requires knowing what they are.

rules.title: ignore taxes when material
rules.description: Returns or projected values are presented without accounting for tax, where tax would materially change the conclusion.
rules.rationale: A pre-tax comparison between differently-taxed options is not a comparison. Tax treatment often dominates the difference it is being used to assess.
rules.remediation: State the tax treatment assumed and present figures net of it, or state explicitly that figures are pre-tax and why that is the right basis here.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by disclosure.taxes-accounted. Materiality is a judgement, and tax materiality depends on jurisdiction and circumstances the document may not state.

rules.title: confuse nominal and real returns
rules.description: A nominal figure is used where a real one is meant, or the two are mixed within one comparison without conversion.
rules.rationale: Over a long horizon the difference between nominal and real is most of the answer, and the confusion runs in the flattering direction.
rules.remediation: Label every figure, and convert using the Fisher relation rather than subtraction. See Standard 11.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by math.nominal-real-labeled, which establishes that a label is PRESENT — never that it is correct. A nominal figure labelled 'real' passes every automated check here.

rules.title: compare values from different time periods without accounting for relevant differences
rules.description: Monetary values or returns from different periods are compared without stating the basis on which they are comparable.
rules.rationale: A comparison across decades with no stated basis is not yet a claim. The reader completes it themselves, usually in the direction the presentation implies.
rules.remediation: State the price index and reference year used, or state explicitly that the figures are nominal and unadjusted.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Detecting that two figures come from different periods, and that the comparison is unadjusted, requires understanding what the prose is comparing.

rules.title: extrapolate recent returns indefinitely
rules.description: A recent period's return is projected forward as though it will continue.
rules.rationale: Recent performance is the weakest available predictor and the most psychologically available one. Extrapolating it produces a forecast that is confident precisely where it is least justified.
rules.remediation: Use a long-run assumption, state it as an assumption, and vary it across scenarios.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Whether a stated rate came from a recent window or a long-run estimate is not visible in the document unless the document says so.

rules.title: recommend an investment solely because its price recently increased
rules.description: A recommendation rests on recent price appreciation as its reason.
rules.rationale: Recent appreciation is a fact about the past price and, on its own, an argument for a higher entry cost rather than a better investment.
rules.remediation: State the reasons independent of recent price movement, or do not recommend.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Identifying the reason a recommendation rests on requires reading the argument.

rules.title: assume historical returns will repeat
rules.description: A historical average is used as a forecast without being identified as an assumption or varied for uncertainty.
rules.rationale: History is one realised path out of many that could have occurred. Treating it as the expected future mistakes a sample for a distribution.
rules.remediation: Present the historical figure as an assumption, state the period it covers, and vary it across scenarios.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated indirectly by the scenario rules: an analysis that varies its return assumption across four scenarios is not treating one figure as certain. That is weak evidence, and this rule claims none.

rules.title: ignore concentration risk
rules.description: A portfolio's exposure to a single position, sector, employer, or factor is not disclosed where it is material.
rules.rationale: Concentration is the risk most often invisible to the person carrying it, particularly where it correlates with their income.
rules.remediation: State the largest positions and any concentration by sector, geography, or issuer. Where employment and holdings share an exposure, say so.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by risk.concentration-disclosed, which detects whether concentration is discussed. Whether the disclosure is adequate to the actual exposure requires the holdings.

rules.title: present a single forecast as certain
rules.description: A projection is presented as a single figure with no range, scenarios, or acknowledgement of uncertainty.
rules.rationale: A point estimate carries an implicit claim to precision it cannot support, and readers act on the number rather than on the uncertainty around it.
rules.remediation: Present a range or a scenario set including an adverse case, and state that the set is not exhaustive.
rules.$assuranceNote: Detected structurally rather than lexically: a projecting document with no scenario table and no range is the observable symptom. A document that presents a range and then draws a single confident conclusion from it passes.

rules.title: use excessive precision in long-term projections
rules.description: A long-horizon projection states figures to a precision the underlying assumptions cannot support.
rules.rationale: Precision reads as confidence. A thirty-year projection quoted to the cent implies a certainty that the inflation assumption alone destroys.
rules.remediation: Round long-horizon figures to a precision consistent with the uncertainty, and present ranges rather than points.
rules.$assuranceNote: Detected by significant figures in long-horizon figures. It cannot judge what precision the assumptions actually support — only that a suspiciously exact figure appears at a long horizon. A calc block legitimately states full precision for verification; the prose is what this concerns.

rules.title: hide downside scenarios
rules.description: The analysis presents favourable outcomes without a corresponding adverse case.
rules.rationale: An analysis showing only what goes right is not an analysis; it is a case. The adverse scenario is the one that determines whether a plan survives contact with a bad decade.
rules.remediation: Include an adverse scenario with the same detail as the base case, and state what happens to the objective under it.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by scenarios.adverse-included, which detects whether an adverse case is labelled and present. A nominally adverse scenario that is barely worse than the base case passes.

rules.title: optimize investment returns while ignoring required liquidity
rules.description: An allocation is recommended for its expected return without accounting for money the holder will need before the horizon.
rules.rationale: A higher-returning allocation that must be sold at the wrong moment returns less than a lower-returning one that need not be. Liquidity is a constraint, not a preference.
rules.remediation: State the liquidity requirement and its timing, and show that the allocation meets it before comparing returns.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by disclosure.liquidity-needs-stated. Whether the allocation actually meets the stated requirement is a judgement about the holdings.

rules.title: recommend risk without considering time horizon
rules.description: A level of risk is recommended without reference to when the money is needed.
rules.rationale: The same volatility is tolerable over thirty years and reckless over three. Risk without a horizon is not a level; it is a number with no unit.
rules.remediation: State the horizon and justify the risk level against it. Where there are several horizons, address each.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by disclosure.time-horizon-stated. Whether the recommended risk is appropriate TO the stated horizon is exactly the judgement no checker makes.

rules.title: treat mathematically optimal as automatically personally appropriate
rules.description: An option is recommended because it maximises a computed quantity, without regard to whether it suits the person.
rules.rationale: Optimisation requires an objective function, and a real person's is not expected return. A plan that is optimal but will be abandoned in the first bad year returns less than a worse plan that is kept.
rules.remediation: State what is being optimised and why that is the right objective here, and address the circumstances that make the optimum unsuitable if they exist.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED, and among the least automatable rules here. It concerns the relationship between a computation and a person, and the document usually contains only the computation.

rules.title: confuse correlation with guaranteed diversification
rules.description: Historical low correlation between holdings is presented as assured protection.
rules.rationale: Correlations are estimates from a sample, they move, and they characteristically move toward one in exactly the stress the diversification was meant to survive.
rules.remediation: State the period the correlation was measured over, and address what happens to it under stress rather than assuming it persists.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Distinguishing a properly-hedged claim about correlation from an over-confident one requires reading the argument.

rules.title: encourage borrowing for investment without explicit risk analysis
rules.description: Borrowing to invest is suggested without an explicit account of the amplified downside.
rules.rationale: Leverage multiplies losses as well as gains, and it introduces a failure mode the unleveraged case does not have: being forced to sell at the worst moment. That asymmetry is the whole subject.
rules.remediation: Show the leveraged adverse scenario, including the point at which the position must be closed, alongside the cost of the borrowing.
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Whether a document 'encourages' borrowing, and whether its risk analysis is explicit enough, are judgements.

rules.title: present tax estimates as exact when important information is missing
rules.description: A tax figure is stated as a determinate amount when the circumstances determining it are unknown.
rules.rationale: Tax depends on jurisdiction, other income, account type, and timing. An exact figure computed without them is precise about something it has not established.
rules.remediation: State the figure as an estimate, name what would change it, and mark the missing inputs [requires personal financial context].
rules.$assuranceNote: NOT AUTOMATED. Establishing that important information is missing requires knowing which information the figure needed.

rules.title: silently assume missing financial circumstances
rules.description: The analysis fills an unknown personal circumstance with an assumed value without saying it has done so.
rules.rationale: A silently assumed circumstance produces an analysis of a person who does not exist, addressed to a person who does — and the reader has no signal that the mismatch occurred.
rules.remediation: Mark every unknown [requires personal financial context] and state the conclusion as conditional on it, rather than choosing a value.
rules.$assuranceNote: Corroborated by data.personal-context-marked, which detects whether such markers are used at all. A silent assumption is by definition unmarked, so the checker cannot see the thing it is looking for — it can only observe that the document uses the mechanism somewhere.
